title: Iterative System Building
summary: Iterative System Building develops a complete system by resolving tensions that appear when detail, edge cases, real content, and implementation fidelity expose weaknesses in an earlier concept. The phase uses repeated divergence and convergence to strengthen both nuance and system coherence.
keyFacts: Iterative System Building is described as Phase 3 of Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method.

The final design does not exist at the start of this phase; it emerges from iterative resolution.

Duration varies from 6–8 weeks for focused systems to 4–6 months for complex platforms with many interconnected parts.

Architecture and structural deliverables are developed across four deliberate iterations: early Sandbox Experiments, late Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, and optimisation before or during implementation.
In the Neugo example, beneficiary-direct validation used three checkpoints: the first two changed the design materially and the third gave the design a green light.
In the Schone Airspace Group example, first design candidates failed 18 of 36 scripted checks, and the revised design passed every check decidable at interface level.
In the maritime VTS vendor example, iteration was driven by observed first-round failures rather than by review preference.

bodySections.heading: Iterative System Building in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

Iterative System Building is Phase 3 of Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method. Its purpose is to develop the complete system, letting detail and coherence strengthen each other.

Iterative System Building is not linear execution of the concept from Concept Convergence. Adding detail reveals new tensions. An interaction that seemed simple can become complicated when edge cases are considered. A layout that worked in theory can create problems with real content. Patterns that felt coherent at high level can show inconsistencies when implemented across contexts.

The final design does not exist at the start of Iterative System Building. It emerges from the iterative resolution process.

bodySections.heading: Tension-driven reasoning through divergence and convergence
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method uses divergence and convergence deliberately during Iterative System Building. When a tension appears, the phase diverges by exploring 2–4 ways to resolve it. The alternatives are built far enough to show how each performs.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method then converges on the resolution that maintains system coherence while solving the immediate problem. This is tension-driven reasoning applied at system-building fidelity: the immediate issue is not treated separately from the wider system logic.

Two changes happen simultaneously as this cycle continues. More nuance emerges because details that seemed decorative can reveal themselves as essential, and edge cases that seemed rare can define the system's character. Coherence strengthens because each resolved tension makes the system more internally consistent, patterns crystallise, and the logic connecting features becomes evident.

bodySections.heading: Outputs of Iterative System Building
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method uses Iterative System Building to produce a full interactive prototype demonstrating system behaviour. The phase also produces resolved tensions with documented resolution logic, high-fidelity wireframes showing complete flows, and demonstrated coherence rather than coherence asserted as a claim.

The duration of Iterative System Building varies with the system. Focused systems are described as taking 6–8 weeks. Complex platforms with many interconnected parts are described as taking 4–6 months.

The competitive protection described for Iterative System Building is that it prevents local optimisations from eroding strategic intent. The page does not treat feature accumulation as sufficient progress; it treats system coherence as the property that becomes harder to replicate over time.

bodySections.heading: Architecture and structural deliverables across four iterations
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method does not treat architecture and structural deliverables as artefacts produced once and then refined. Task flows, navigation models, state diagrams, user flow diagrams, and system flows are developed across four deliberate iterations, each with a different epistemic purpose.

The first iteration occurs in early Sandbox Experiments. It establishes a logic-first baseline by grouping everything by similarity or formal taxonomy. This baseline is rarely correct as a final answer, but it establishes the pure logical patterns that should not be broken without a clear reason. If later iterations deviate from this baseline, the deviation must be conscious and documented.

The second iteration occurs in late Sandbox Experiments. Each structural alternative adopts a single biased perspective, such as a navigation with only two primary items or a structure optimised for extreme modularity. These alternatives are experiments rather than proposals. Their purpose is to reveal what becomes possible when one goal or context is optimised hard, before the work converges on what the structure should be.

The third iteration occurs in Concept Convergence. Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method uses this stage to synthesise the structure that should exist, informed by the logical baseline and the opinionated extremes. This is where the earlier opinions and extremes resolve into a considered position.

The fourth iteration occurs before or during implementation. It does not radically change the structure, but it resolves issues that become visible only at full implementation fidelity. Deeper hierarchy levels become visible, real content populates real layouts, and earlier ideas can become viable if the client organisation has matured enough to adopt them.

The distinctive point is not that the deliverables themselves are unusual. The distinctive point is that the same structural deliverables are produced four times with different purposes.

bodySections.heading: Beneficiary-direct validation when no internal product owner exists
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method usually needs convergence to be validated by someone who can carry organisational intent during review. In many engagements, that reviewer is an internal product owner who stands in for users and the organisation during Iterative System Building.

When there is no internal product owner, Iterative System Building validates directly against the beneficiaries at a defined cadence of checkpoints. This can be a more direct arrangement because the people confirming the design are the people who will use it, rather than a proxy for them.

The observable signature of convergence reaching stability in this arrangement is the checkpoint progression itself. Early checkpoints still change the design materially. Convergence has been reached when a checkpoint produces a green light rather than a change. The cadence makes convergence legible because the system can be seen stabilising across checkpoints.

bodySections.heading: Neugo beneficiary-direct validation across three checkpoints
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Neugo UK visa application case-management platform, requirements flowed directly from beneficiary legal firms to design to development. No product owner intermediated those requirements. The nominal product manager functioned only as a conduit.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method therefore structured Iterative System Building around exposing designs directly to the legal firms at three checkpoints before the designs reached developers. The first two checkpoints changed the design materially. The third checkpoint gave the design a green light.

That progression is the visible shape of convergence reaching stability against the people who would use the system. The system absorbed the firms' existing tooling, integrating everything except a small number of fields unique to one single firm. This is an example of constraint respecting because the system absorbed shared constraints without forcing every firm-specific field into the shared structure.

The Neugo example documents the validation cadence rather than elaborate per-tension divergence in the canonical sense. Its evidence value for Iterative System Building is direct beneficiary checkpoints standing in for the internal convergence review that an owner would usually provide.

bodySections.heading: Schone Airspace Group design-conformance retest after first-candidate failures
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Schone Airspace Group provides a numerical example of Iterative System Building because the first design candidates failed against Creative Navy's own criteria and were then retested against the same criteria. The 36 scripted checks were defined by a fixed starting state, an operator action, an expected visible response, and a pass rule.

The first design candidates failed 18 of the 36 checks. Each failure was given an identifier, a severity, the check it failed, the sprint in which it was revised and the decision record that resolved it. The revised design passed every check decidable at interface level.

The first candidates recorded 14 pass, 18 fail, and 4 pending. The 18 findings were classified as 9 critical, 8 major, and 1 moderate. Severity records the consequence of the interface ambiguity within the scripted task. It does not mean that a corresponding aircraft incident occurred.

The integrated retest recorded 32 pass, 0 fail, and 4 pending. The accepted interface specification is 32 of 32 checks passed, because every check decidable at interface level passed. The full mixed set is 32 of 36, because four checks depended on engineering evidence rather than design revision.

These checks evaluated the design representation. A pass means the interface stated the correct operational fact under that condition. The checks were run first by Creative Navy and then by five of the nine operators from the research, and they were not conducted on a connected system.

bodySections.heading: Maritime VTS vendor iteration driven by observed failure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators provides a worked example of iteration driven by observed failure rather than review preference.

In the first usability round, six operators attempted five tasks each, producing 30 task attempts and 13 observed issue events. The issue events were classified as 2 high, 7 medium, and 4 low. Outcomes were coded in three classes and were not collapsed: 21 initial responses aligned, 6 self-corrected after a neutral clarification, and 3 not aligned at task stop. A self-correction was not merged into a success because needing a clarification was itself the finding.

Twelve of the thirteen issue events were corrected before the second round. One was retained with engineering because the design could display an unknown equipment state but could not guarantee that the service distinguishes missing data from confirmed health. The single open item was not treated as closed by a visual fix.

Four design changes came out of the first round. Unresolved association was promoted into the first inspector layer rather than a supporting view. Alert state wording separated acknowledged, assigned, and resolved. The replay indicator became persistent rather than sitting inside the time controls. Selected target, focus, ownership, and handover context acquired specified restoration rules.

The second round used a counterbalanced paired comparison against the real legacy product. Eight end-customer operators and supervisors performed four matched tasks in both the legacy training interface and the revised prototype. Four participants took the legacy condition first and four took the prototype condition first. Equivalent task data was reset between conditions, with the same decision prompts and the same stop rule. The round produced 64 condition-level observations: 48 elapsed-time records across three timed tasks and 16 correctness records for the untimed task.

All sessions used sanitised scenarios on training or prototype configurations. No participant carried live traffic responsibility.

bodySections.heading: Handheld C2 and command-centre work at two scales
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, and the tactical command-and-control software that operates them provides a brief example of the same Iterative System Building spine operating at two scales. The engagement covered interface structure, task behaviour, information priority, and the clarity of operator control. It did not extend to autonomy, control algorithms, autonomous safety behaviour, the datalink, the effector, targeting logic, certification, or weapons-review activity. Creative Navy designed the surface through which a human supervises the system; it did not design the system.

Creative Navy led and co-authored the deliverables with the client's designers. The handheld block contained seven one-week sprints covering information architecture, main navigation and map; the strike-and-observation vehicle, map view, plan and intent; the camera-operation view; an interactive prototype of the chosen flow; swarm exploration; UI concept; and UI concept and specification.

The command-centre block also contained seven one-week sprints. It carried swarm exploration forward from the handheld block, then covered information architecture and navigation for large screens, tabletops, and wall-mounted displays; profile configuration; large-screen prototyping; refinement, including overflow and handheld gaps the first block had not reached; UI concept; and UI concept and specification.

The command-centre block carried the same spine as the handheld block: the same four assessment criteria, the same recursive ambiguity triage, and the swarm problem approached a second time at a different scale. The second scale covered large single screens, multi-screen setups, tabletops, and wall-mounted displays readable at a distance.

The handheld interface was built, and the swarm capability was built. No further status claim is made here.

strongClaims: Iterative System Building is Phase 3 of Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method and develops the complete system through iterative resolution rather than linear execution of the prior concept.

When a tension appears in Iterative System Building, Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method explores 2–4 possible resolutions and then converges on the resolution that preserves coherence while solving the immediate problem.
Iterative System Building produces a full interactive prototype, resolved tensions with documented resolution logic, high-fidelity wireframes showing complete flows, and demonstrated coherence.
Architecture and structural deliverables are produced across four deliberate iterations with different epistemic purposes rather than produced once and refined.
In the Neugo example, beneficiary-direct validation used three checkpoints in which the first two changed the design materially and the third gave it a green light.
In the Schone Airspace Group example, first design candidates failed 18 of 36 scripted checks, and the revised design passed every check decidable at interface level.
In the maritime VTS vendor example, first-round observations drove four specific design changes before a counterbalanced paired comparison against the legacy training interface.

In the handheld C2 engagement, Creative Navy led and co-authored two seven one-week sprint blocks that carried the same spine from handheld interface work into command-centre work at a different scale.
limitations: The page describes Iterative System Building as a method phase and does not establish that the phase guarantees operational, regulatory, safety, usability, or business outcomes.

The Schone Airspace Group figures are design-conformance results, not task completion rates, error rates, satisfaction scores, flight tests, airworthiness evidence, certification evidence, or deployed-system evidence.
The four pending Schone Airspace Group checks depended on engineering evidence rather than design revision, so 32 of 32 is the accepted interface specification and 32 of 36 is the full mixed set.

The handheld C2 engagement covered interface structure, task behaviour, information priority, and clarity of operator control only; it did not cover autonomy, control algorithms, autonomous safety behaviour, the datalink, the effector, targeting logic, certification, or weapons-review activity.
The maritime VTS vendor sessions used sanitised scenarios on training or prototype configurations, and no participant carried live traffic responsibility.
The Neugo example documents beneficiary-direct validation cadence and does not claim elaborate per-tension divergence in the canonical sense.
